summary: Destiny appreciates Duolingo's visual approach to learning ASL, though she wishes the app offered more in-depth cultural context.
top_quotes: Duolingo's pictures and animations really help me remember signs, 'cause I'm a visual learner.
I could use more info on deaf culture, so I understand the context, not just the words.
When I see my daughter signing back to me, that's when I know Duolingo's really workin'.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey there! I'm Destiny, so nice to chat with ya today. Lookin' forward to it!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, I grew up right here in Atlanta, Georgia, sweet as a peach! I've always been the creative type, you know, drawin' and paintin'. Now I'm a proud mama to the most beautiful little girl. Workin' hard as a single mom ain't easy, but she's my world. Got into learnin' ASL 'cause I wanna teach her, too. Always loved the idea of breakin' through language barriers, ya know?

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I grew up right here in Atlanta, been here my whole life.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Atlanta was, and still is, all about community and diversity. It’s like a big family here. Growing up, we had block parties, church on Sundays, and soul food that’d make you wanna slap your mama! It’s a real special place.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Having my daughter was definitely a big turnin' point. I mean, everything changed. Suddenly, I had this little person who depended on me entirely. It made me reassess what really mattered in life and to focus on buildin' a better future for us both.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, it’s like I had this new purpose, you know? Every decision I make now, from work to learnin’ ASL, it’s partly 'cause I wanna be the best mama I can be. It gave me a whole new kinda strength I didn’t know I had.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Took it one day at a time, honestly. Leaned on my family and friends a lot. Sometimes, I’d just steal a quiet moment after she was asleep, say a little prayer, and remind myself to keep pushin'.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I'm all about learnin’ ASL. I want my daughter and I to have this secret language, ya know? Plus, I love the idea of her bein' able to communicate with more folks than just those who speak English.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It builds a bridge, you know? I want her to grow up understanding diversity and inclusivity. Learnin’ ASL is like teachin’ her those values in practice.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day? That's when I get to spend some quality time with my daughter, maybe take her to the park. If I can squeeze in some learnin' time on Duolingo, that’s a cherry on top! Even better if I see her eyes light up when we’re practicin’ together.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: If I’m goin' to bed feelin' like I've accomplished something, like we’ve laughed a lot and learned a little, maybe managed to keep the house clean, that’s a good day.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I lean a lot on my gut. I’m a big feeler, ya know? But I also talk it through with my mom or best friend sometimes. They give me that reality check I need to balance the heart and head.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I’d say I’m a bit of both. Love to plan, but I try to leave room for surprises. Sometimes life has its own ideas, and you just gotta ride that wave.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, like, I planned to take my daughter to the zoo last month, but it rained like cats and dogs! So, we ended up havin' an indoor picnic and movie day at home. Turned out to be even more fun in the end.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to weigh the pros and cons. It’s kinda like walkin’ a tightrope sometimes, you know? Pick carefully, but don’t be afraid to jump if it feels right. I think bein' a mom taught me that sometimes the biggest risks bring the greatest rewards.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: A typical weekday starts bright and early. Gotta get my daughter up and ready for school. Then I’m off to work. After that, it’s errands, cookin’ dinner, and helpin' with homework. I try to fit in some ASL practice with Duolingo before bed. It’s a packed day, but I get a rhythm goin'.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely jugglin’ work and takin' care of my daughter. There are days it feels like there aren’t enough hours, but I remind myself why I’m doin’ it all, and that keeps me goin'.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I would love more time for my art. Miss sittin’ down with my paints and really losin' myself in a canvas. It’s my therapy, and I think I could use a bit more of that balance in my life.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: For sure it’s been time, more than anything. Between work, raisin’ a kid, and just tryin’ to keep up with life, it feels like I'm always runnin'. Wish I had a pause button sometimes!

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I try to plan as much as I can and remind myself to breathe. Sometimes I’ll schedule a ‘do-nothing’ day just to recoup, and that helps recharge my batteries for when real life kicks back in.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I’m closest to my mom and my best friend. They’re my rocks. We’ve been through thick and thin together, and there’s nothin’ I can’t tell them.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: My mom is my hero, really. She’s always there with a word of wisdom or just a hug when I need it. My best friend, she’s like a sister. Always got my back, and we laugh 'til we cry.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Probably at home or work. Home is my sanctuary, and work is where I grind, so it’s a lotta back and forth there.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Home is my safe haven. It’s where I can be myself, relax, and recharge. Work is more about focus and makin’ sure I’m doin’ the best I can to provide for my daughter.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: At home, it’s the comfort and familiarity. At work, it’s the hustle and responsibility, knowing I’m makin’ a difference in our lives.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I turn to my mom first. She’s got a way of calmin’ me down and helpin’ me see things from a different angle. If she ain’t around, my best friend’s the next call.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was a time this past year when I was laid off for a bit. That was real tough. Didn’t know how I was gonna keep the lights on, you know? But somehow, we always find a way through.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was scary, for sure. Made me question a lot, like, what am I gonna do next? But it also pushed me to hustle harder and get creative about findin’ new opportunities.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: Leaned on my faith real hard. Found strength in prayer and took it all one day at a time. My family was a huge support, too, and just knowin’ I had them helped ease the burden.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Breathin’ deeply, honestly. Sometimes I just close my eyes and count to ten. When I can, I paint or sketch. It lets me express what I'm feelin’ without words.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be even more stable, secure, and satisfied. Maybe own a little place with a backyard for my daughter. Wanna be fluent in ASL so we can help bridge communication barriers wherever we go.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: Would love to have a bit more financial freedom, and definitely more time for myself and my family. And I’d like to be even more involved in the deaf community as an advocate.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I tried a few online videos and some books, but it was hard to stay consistent. I’m a visual learner, so just reading about signs didn’t really stick. Needed something interactive, ya know?

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The pace was often either too slow or too fast, and I needed more visuals. Plus, it felt kinda isolating tryin’ to learn from a book or video without interaction.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was a time I tried to sign ‘thank you’ to a friend’s deaf child, but I fumbled it so bad. That’s when I knew I needed somethin’ more effective, somethin’ that would really stick.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I heard about it from a friend who was using it to learn Spanish. She said it was super easy to use and fun, so I thought I’d give it a try.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I liked the idea of it bein’ on my phone, so I could practice anytime, anywhere. Plus, the visual and interactive elements seemed like a perfect match for me.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: So, last night, after tuckin' in my daughter, I opened Duolingo and got to the ASL lesson. They started with a review of signs, using these cute little animations and pictures that really help me grasp the signs. I love how it prompts you to match signs with images, then tests you with short quizzes. Makes it feel like a game, not a chore. Afterward, I even tried a couple of the signs with my daughter to see if we could remember together.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, it’s the visuals and the way they repeat the signs in different contexts. It helps me lock it in my brain. I love that it's like a game, keeps me engaged without overthinkin'.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes, it’s when the lessons don’t give much context. Like, I’d love to know more about when or why a sign is used culturally. Feel like I’m missin’ the backstory sometimes, ya know?

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: The times when the app freezes or doesn’t sync my progress. I’ll think I’ve completed a module, but then I gotta do it all over again. That’s when I’m tempted to throw my phone out the window!

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Oh mercy, I was feelin' accomplished one night, finished a whole section. Closed my app, went back the next day, and it looked like I hadn’t done it. Felt like my work just disappeared. Had to redo the whole thing. That was a ‘grit-your-teeth-and-bear-it’ moment.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes I’ll use YouTube to find videos that give more cultural context. Also, there are Facebook groups I joined where I can ask questions and get tips from other ASL learners.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me community and context. It’s one thing to learn a vocabulary, but I wanna understand how to use the language fluidly in real-life situations.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case? I’d be usin’ the wrong signs in a conversation and end up offendin’ someone. That’s why I crave more cultural insight along with the langauge.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it’ll make me feel like I’m makin’ progress—like, every time I open it, I want to walk away knowin’ I’ve got a new tool in my communication toolbox.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I see my daughter signing back to me and understandin' what I’m sayin’, that’s when I know it’s workin'. It’s like magic, truly.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I’d add more lessons on deaf culture. It’s just as important as the language itself, and I think learnin’ it together would make a world of difference.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: More community involvement in language learning. Maybe in-person meetups or virtual hangouts that bring learners together to practice and share stories.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Not really, just wanna say it’s been nice sharin’ this with y’all. The journey’s not just about me learnin’ but also inspirin' my daughter to be a lifelong learner.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure thing, y’all go ahead! Just make sure she’s got a good sense of humor like me!
